doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: The changing scene; clinics, trombone days and many hats
summary: Raph talks about his 50th Street studio, his clinics for King/UMI, trombone days in Ireland and Australia, church organ, the union local, the brass band and writing for Carl Fischer.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Can you, on that limited basis, can you tell how has the scene changed in the last ten years, or has it? You know this is not really new, but electronics replacing—

Oh okay. Well we all went through that. I never considered myself a barometer of the business, even at my busiest. There were always guys that were busier and that knew more than I did about the business, and especially now I’m certainly nowhere near being able to put an accurate handle on it. But the way it seems to me is guys are working a little bit harder and they’re going out of town a little bit more — the good guys — they’re really traveling a bit more, they’re doing a little more road work than, at one point, than I used to. Because I could maintain — I had a studio in town on 50th Street and 7th Avenue. I had that studio for 25 years. I kept all my instruments there. I never once brought an instrument home, because I had instruments home and I had instruments there, and I just used what’s there. Warm-up in the morning, go out, work during the day and do what I had to. I’ve always done clinics and solos for King instruments, which is now United Musical Instruments. So I’m playing a King, a Benge and also a Conn on occasion. I’m doing things for them still. Last year we went to Ireland and we had the first ever trombone day in Bantry, Ireland, which I set up. The year before we went to Australia and I did a couple of clinics in Western Australia. I’m bringing my brass band to Australia this coming summer, 2002, and I’m going trombone day number two in Bantry in three months, in February. All of this, you know, is sort of a reflection on my doing clinics and solos. It’s that particular hat that I’m wearing. And United Musical Instruments has been sponsoring a little bit of that. They’ve been helpful. I dropped the ball there somewhere with the conversation.
Oh, we were just talking about the state of the business I guess.

I’ve always gone my own way. I’ve always done what I thought would be helpful to me. I’ve tried to get as much experience as I could in all types of music and then hopefully cash in on that experience. I’ve done that. Whereas most of the guys in a particular band would be of a particular type of musician doing certain types of work, I always found that I was doing other stuff, which is one of the reasons that I probably don’t talk too much to A about B or left hand about what the right hand is doing. I just kind of keep everything in its own place. I wear a lot of hats. I play church organ these days. I’m playing at a Maronite church in Danbury, I’m president of the musician’s union, the local A F of M local 87 in Danbury, and I have the brass band as I mentioned. But I wear a lot of different hats. I do the trombone and the tuba and keyboard and teaching and writing. I have something — I have about eight or nine things out with Carl Fisher and there’s
something in the works right now and there’s another thing that we’re talking about so I’ve been doing a bit of writing for them.
